newsitem.title: PERU: Fujimori says no return to the past for Peru.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori says no return to the past for Peru.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori said on Monday that the 34-day stand-off between his government and Marxists holding 73 hostages in Lima will not send Peru back to its bloody past or jeopardise economic reform.
"The Peruvian people do not want to go backwards nor accept a return of violence and disorder to the country," Fujimori said in speeches to welcome two new ambassadors to Peru.
"The peace and stability achieved are the pillars of our development ... There exists the widest possible consensus among the population with regard to the need for peace and stability."
In six years of power, Fujimori virtually defeated leftist guerrillas waging armed conflict since 1980 and transformed the Peruvian economy along free-market lines.
Before the guerrilla movements were suppressed, an estimated 30,000 people were killed after 1980 in conflicts involving the government against the MRTA and larger Maoist Shining Path movements.

But the spectacular Dec. 17 takeover of the Japanese ambassador's residence by Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels claiming to represent the poor revived memories of Peru's past and threatened to set back Fujimori's achievements.
Fujimori said the crisis would cause a minimum of damage to the nation.
"The isolated event of the takeover of the Japanese ambassador's residence and the kidnapping of 73 people are not going to change our national direction," he said.

"Peru has converted itself into one of the region's most attractive emerging markets ... Investments in our country are totally guaranteed and the flow of investments has not stopped, proof that confidence in the country remains."
The government and MRTA rebels holding the diplomatic residence remained deadlocked on Monday as the 73 hostages spent their 34th day under the gun.
Both sides said they were ready to talk but a face-to-face meeting was on hold because the goverment ruled out considering the MRTA's main demand: the release of jailed comrades.
International Committee of the Red Cross representative Michel Minnig spent about three hours inside the besieged residence on Monday in what appeared to be a routine visit, witnesses said.

Several dozen former policemen, some in wheelchairs and all wounded in one way or another in the government's fight against rebel groups, held a demonstration at the siege site to demand freedom for the hostages.
Reinforcing Peru's unflinching stand against the MRTA, Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto vowed on Monday never to give in to "terrorism."

"Terrorist activity is a grave challenge to all states and societies and it is vital for the international community to tackle terrorism in unity," Hashimoto said in a speech to Japan's parliament in Tokyo.
He reiterated his "complete confidence" in Fujimori's refusal to discuss the release of 400 jailed MRTA members.

The rebels have started to use the captives as workhands. One of the hostages spent nearly an hour on Sunday removing batteries from cars parked outside the building, which the rebels apparently planned to use to power their radios.
Peruvian daily Expreso reported on Monday that MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini was communicating with fellow rebels throughout Peru via coded radio messages.

"The messages that are being sent from the radio, according to the police, are camouflaged through a system of binary numbers whose content is only know by Cerpa and the comrades backing him up from outside the residence," Expreso said, adding the code system was changed every week.

The remaining hostages inside the residence include about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats, Peruvian government and security force officials, two ambassadors, and Fujimori's younger brother, Pedro.
